question: Should I buy an online trading course?
short: Usually not. Most paid trading courses sell the dream of quitting your job, and the income screenshots come from the few who got lucky.
flags: Income screenshots and lifestyle photos are marketing, not proof that students make money.
Countdown timers and "only 3 spots left" are pressure tactics. Real education doesn't expire tonight.
Many courses upsell signals groups, coaching or a "pro" tier once you're in.
alt: Learn the basics free from your broker's education pages, library books and regulator guides, and practise on a demo account for three months before spending anything.
checks: Ask for audited results of typical students, not the best ones.
Get the refund policy in writing before you pay.
Search the course name plus "scam", "refund" and "reddit".
q: Online trading course for $1,500, 50% off today only

question: Should I buy the extended warranty?
short: Usually no. Extended warranties are priced so the store makes money on them, and most products don't break in the extra years they cover.
flags: Many credit cards already add an extra year of warranty to purchases.
The fine print often excludes the things that actually break, like batteries and accidental damage.
The sales push at the till is a sign of how profitable these plans are.
alt: Put the warranty money in a savings pot for repairs. If you are clumsy with phones, compare the maker's own accident plan instead of the store's.
checks: Check what the manufacturer's warranty already covers.
Check your credit card's purchase protection.
Read exactly what is excluded before deciding.
q: Extended 3-year warranty for $199 on a $900 laptop

question: Should I buy a used car without an inspection?
short: No. An independent pre-purchase inspection costs a little and can save you thousands. A seller who won't allow one is telling you something.
flags: Hidden accident damage, flood damage and failing gearboxes don't show on a test drive.
"Sold as seen" means you have little comeback after you pay.
Pressure to decide today is a reason to slow down.
alt: Pay for an independent inspection and a vehicle history report, or choose a certified pre-owned car with a warranty.
checks: Run the vehicle history report for accidents, write-offs and mileage.
Book an independent mechanic, not one the seller suggests.
Compare the total price, not the monthly payment.
q: Used 2018 SUV, 70,000 miles, $16,000, seller says no time for an inspection

question: Should I buy the new iPhone or last year's model?
short: If your phone works, last year's model or a refurbished one does nearly everything for a lot less. Buy new only if a specific new feature matters to you.
flags: Year-to-year upgrades are usually small. Check what's actually different for how you use it.
0% financing makes the price feel smaller but locks you in for years.
Trade-in offers often pay less than selling your old phone yourself.
alt: A manufacturer-refurbished or last-generation model with a full warranty, often 20 to 30% cheaper.
checks: List the two features you'd actually use every day.
Compare the refurbished price from the maker's own store.
Price your old phone on a resale site before accepting a trade-in.
q: New iPhone Pro on 0% financing, $1,199, my current phone still works

question: Should I buy a mattress on a "today only" sale?
short: Mattress sales run most of the year, so "today only" rarely is. If you need a new mattress, buy one with a long home trial instead of chasing the deadline.
flags: The list price is often set high so the sale price looks like a bargain.
Returns can be expensive or have pick-up fees. Check before you buy.
Showroom tests of a few minutes tell you little about sleeping on it for months.
alt: A well-reviewed online mattress with a 100-night trial and free returns.
checks: Find out how long the trial is and who pays for a return.
Check the price history if the store lets you.
Read the 1-star reviews for sagging and durability complaints.

question: Should I buy a crypto trading bot?
short: No. Bots and signal groups promising steady daily returns match the most common investment scam pattern. Nobody sells a machine that prints money.
flags: Guaranteed or steady daily returns are the classic sign of a scam.
Many of these platforms let money in but make withdrawals difficult or impossible.
If you're asked to recruit friends or deposit more to unlock profits, walk away.
alt: If you want to invest, a low-cost, regulated index fund. If you're already in, try a small withdrawal now and report the platform to your regulator if it fails.
checks: Search your financial regulator's warning list for the company name.
Never send money to someone you met through a DM.
Talk to a qualified financial adviser before investing large sums.
q: Crypto trading bot an influencer DMed me, guaranteed 2% a day

question: Should I use buy now, pay later?
short: It's fine for something you could pay for today anyway. It's a problem when it's the only way you can afford it, because the payments stack up.
flags: Several small plans at once add up fast and are easy to lose track of.
Missed payments can bring late fees and may affect your credit.
Splitting the price makes impulse buys feel cheaper than they are.
alt: Wait until you can pay in full. If it's still worth it after saving for a few weeks, buy it then.
checks: Add up every plan you already have running.
Read the late fee terms.
Ask: would I buy this if I had to pay all of it today?
q: Designer jacket $600 in 4 payments with Klarna

question: Should I buy a timeshare?
short: Almost always no. Timeshares come with yearly fees that tend to rise, they're hard to resell, and the sales presentations are built around pressure.
flags: Annual maintenance fees continue for years and often go up.
Resale values are typically far below what buyers paid.
"Free" gifts for attending a presentation are bait for a high-pressure pitch.
alt: Book holiday rentals as you go. You keep your money and your freedom to go somewhere else next year.
checks: Check the cooling-off period where you are, and use it if you've signed.
Look up resale listings for the same resort.
Never sign on the day of the presentation.
q: Timeshare presentation, $25,000 with a free cruise if I sign today

question: Should I buy a refurbished laptop?
short: Often yes, if it's refurbished by the maker or a reputable seller with a real warranty. You can get a much better laptop for the same money.
flags: "Refurbished" means different things. Check who did the work.
Battery health varies. Ask for the battery condition or a replacement guarantee.
Avoid sellers with no warranty or a very short return window.
alt: Buy manufacturer-certified refurbished first; it usually comes with the same warranty as new.
checks: Confirm the warranty length and who honours it.
Check the model year so it still gets software updates.
Test everything in the return window: ports, keyboard, screen, battery.

question: Should I buy a supplement I saw on TikTok?
short: Be very careful. Supplements don't have to prove they work before they're sold, and creator videos are usually paid ads.
flags: Before-and-after videos and testimonials aren't evidence.
"Subscribe and save" can quietly turn into monthly charges.
Some supplements interact with medicines. Check with a pharmacist or doctor first.
alt: Ask a pharmacist what has real evidence for your goal. It's often a cheap, plain product.
checks: Look for independent third-party testing on the label.
Check if the creator is sponsored.
Read the cancellation terms before subscribing.
q: $65 a month gut health gummies from a TikTok ad

question: Should I buy a dropshipping mentorship?
short: Usually not. The person selling the mentorship often makes more from selling mentorships than from dropshipping.
flags: Revenue screenshots show sales, not profit after ads, refunds and fees.
Much of the material is available free on YouTube and blogs.
High-ticket coaching often comes with pressure to pay for more tiers.
alt: Spend a month on free material and test one product with a small ad budget you can afford to lose. You'll learn more for far less.
checks: Ask for proof of profit, not revenue.
Get the refund policy in writing.
Find past students who aren't affiliates.

question: Should I finance a car over 84 months?
short: Usually no. A seven-year loan lowers the monthly payment but raises the total you pay, and you can owe more than the car is worth for years.
flags: Longer loans usually mean more interest in total.
You may be "underwater" (owing more than it's worth) for much of the loan.
The low monthly figure can push you into a more expensive car than you need.
alt: A cheaper car over a shorter loan, with financing arranged through your own bank or credit union before visiting the dealer.
checks: Ask for the total cost of the loan, all payments added up.
Get a quote from your own bank first.
Compare the same car over 48 or 60 months.
q: New SUV $45,000 financed over 84 months at $650 a month
